title: Policy-as-code enforcement
subtitle: Policy in my governance platform is enforced by hooks, not remembered by prompts: a lead cannot edit an artifact, work cannot dispatch before its evidence exists, a hook may never report an operation that did not happen.

stats.label: hook modules served by one binary
shell hooks it replaced, ported with tests

lede: In AgentOS I found that long agent runs fail because the agent is asked to remember the rules along with everything else. I moved the rules out of the agent and into code that runs inside its runtime, in the hook points the agent cannot route around. The coding tools I govern expose lifecycle hooks, before a tool call, after one, at session start, when the agent tries to stop. One Rust binary serves all of them. The diagnosis is in Why long agent runs fail. A publisher writes the hook configuration into each agent environment and checks it byte for byte, so the rules that run are the rules I wrote. The effects are what matter.
quote: I turn an operating procedure into enforcement an autonomous agent cannot ignore, and I phrase each refusal so it teaches the next correct step.
evidence: Policy-as-code for AI agents: about 100 hook modules across 11 lifecycle events in one Rust binary, ported from 63 shell hooks, enforcing rules inside the agent runtime.
Multi-agent governance: ratified work orders locked to the operator, agents confined to their assigned paths, and refusals that name only a command that exists for that agent.
Configuration integrity: hook configuration published into every agent environment with a byte-for-byte check against the approved copy.
Incident-driven guardrails: a test that wrote into the real database became a source-scanning rule that fails the build on any unapproved database connection.
author: Corey James
